claim: Termites build complex nests which are an impressive example of self-organization.
source: Termites build complex nests which are an impressive example of self-organization.
evidence: This is a general statement about termite behavior that draws from established scientific understanding of termite nest construction.

claim: The coordinated actions involved in the construction of termite nests by multiple individuals are primarily mediated by signals and cues embedded in the structure of the nest itself.
source: We know that the coordinated actions involved in the construction of these nests by multiple individuals are primarily mediated by signals and cues embedded in the structure of the nest itself.
evidence: This statement reflects established scientific consensus about stigmergic coordination in termite nest building.

claim: There is no scientific consensus about the nature of the stimuli that guide termite construction and how they are sensed by termites.
source: However, to date there is still no scientific consensus about the nature of the stimuli that guide termite construction, and how they are sensed by termites.
evidence: This claim is supported by the review of conflicting literature presented in the introduction section.

claim: Pellet collections were evenly distributed across the experimental setup in Coptotermes gestroi termites.
source: Pellet collections were evenly distributed across the experimental setup, compatible with a collection mechanism that is not affected by local topography, but only by the distribution of termite occupancy (termites pick pellets at the positions where they are).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Pellet depositions were concentrated at locations of high surface curvature and at the boundaries between different types of substrate.
source: Conversely, pellet depositions were concentrated at locations of high surface curvature and at the boundaries between different types of substrate.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A, 2B, and 2C.

claim: All pellet deposition regions correspond to local maxima in the evaporation flux.
source: The single feature shared by all pellet deposition regions was that they correspond to local maxima in the evaporation flux.
evidence: This is supported by both analytical calculations and chemical garden experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Evaporation flux is directly proportional to the local curvature of nest surfaces.
source: We can show analytically and we confirm experimentally that evaporation flux is directly proportional to the local curvature of nest surfaces.
evidence: This is demonstrated through mathematical derivation in Appendix 2 and confirmed by chemical garden experiments in Figure 4.

claim: Surface curvature is sufficient to organize termite building activity.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that surface curvature is sufficient to organize termite building activity and that termites likely sense curvature indirectly through substrate evaporation.
evidence: This conclusion is based on experimental observations and computational simulations shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Termites likely sense curvature indirectly through substrate evaporation.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that surface curvature is sufficient to organize termite building activity and that termites likely sense curvature indirectly through substrate evaporation.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between evaporation patterns and deposition behavior, supported by chemical garden experiments.

claim: Termites rely on individual memory and proprioception to guide their behavior.
source: Termites rely on individual memory and proprioception to guide their behavior (see e.g. Bardunias and Su, 2009a), but these individual abilities are considered not sufficient to explain nest construction more generally.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by Bardunias and Su, 2009a.

claim: Individual memory and proprioception are not sufficient to explain nest construction in termites.
source: Termites rely on individual memory and proprioception to guide their behavior (see e.g. Bardunias and Su, 2009a), but these individual abilities are considered not sufficient to explain nest construction more generally.
evidence: This reflects established scientific consensus in the field.

claim: Building activity is largely guided by signals and cues embedded directly in the structure of the nest itself through stigmergy.
source: Instead, it is believed that building activity is largely guided by signals and cues embedded directly in the structure of the nest itself, through a regulation principle identified for the first time by Grassé, who named it stigmergy (Grassé, 1959; Camazine et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational work by Grassé, 1959 and Camazine et al., 2001.

claim: Grassé first identified the regulation principle of stigmergy.
source: Instead, it is believed that building activity is largely guided by signals and cues embedded directly in the structure of the nest itself, through a regulation principle identified for the first time by Grassé, who named it stigmergy (Grassé, 1959; Camazine et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation to Grassé, 1959.

claim: Bruinsma, 1979 found evidence for the role of a building pheromone released by the queen in the construction of the royal chamber of Macrotermes subhyalinus.
source: Bruinsma, 1979 found evidence for the role of a building pheromone released by the queen in the construction of the royal chamber of the termite Macrotermes subhyalinus.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bruinsma, 1979.

claim: Computer simulation studies assume the existence of a 'cement pheromone' added to the building material.
source: Computer simulation studies, aimed at reproducing the building behavior of termites and ants, also assume the existence of a "cement pheromone" added to the building material (Khuong et al., 2011; Khuong et al., 2016; Heyde et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Khuong et al., 2011; Khuong et al., 2016; Heyde et al., 2021.

claim: The main role of a cement pheromone in simulation studies is to allow initial pellet depositions to continue growing by differentiating them from regions of pellet collection.
source: In these simulation studies, the main and essential role of a cement pheromone is to allow initial pellet depositions to continue growing by differentiating them from regions of pellet collection, through differential pheromone marking.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited simulation studies.

claim: Experimental evidence in support for cement pheromone in termite construction is weak.
source: Experimental evidence in support for such cement pheromone in termite construction is weak: while individual workers can recognize freshly deposited nest material, they could simply be attracted to an unspecific colony odor while exhibiting the same behavioral patterns that they would exhibit also in the absence of chemical marking (Petersen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Petersen et al., 2015 and represents an inference about the state of evidence.

claim: Individual termite workers can recognize freshly deposited nest material.
source: Experimental evidence in support for such cement pheromone in termite construction is weak: while individual workers can recognize freshly deposited nest material, they could simply be attracted to an unspecific colony odor while exhibiting the same behavioral patterns that they would exhibit also in the absence of chemical marking (Petersen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Petersen et al., 2015.

claim: Elevation is a strong stimulus that could guide termite construction activity.
source: Recent experimental studies by various authors have indicated that morphological and environmental features associated with some nest structures are strong stimuli that could by themselves guide termite construction activity. These include elevation (Fouquet et al., 2014), humidity gradients (Soar et al., 2019), and surface curvature (Calovi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fouquet et al., 2014.

claim: Humidity gradients are a strong stimulus that could guide termite construction activity.
source: Recent experimental studies by various authors have indicated that morphological and environmental features associated with some nest structures are strong stimuli that could by themselves guide termite construction activity. These include elevation (Fouquet et al., 2014), humidity gradients (Soar et al., 2019), and surface curvature (Calovi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Soar et al., 2019.

claim: Surface curvature is a strong stimulus that could guide termite construction activity.
source: Recent experimental studies by various authors have indicated that morphological and environmental features associated with some nest structures are strong stimuli that could by themselves guide termite construction activity. These include elevation (Fouquet et al., 2014), humidity gradients (Soar et al., 2019), and surface curvature (Calovi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Calovi et al., 2019.

claim: The strong attractiveness of digging sites for termite aggregation means that digging and deposition actions mostly come in pairs.
source: The strong attractiveness of digging sites for termite aggregation means that in all these studies digging and deposition actions mostly come in pairs, which prevents us from identifying the genuine cues for pellet collection and deposition (Bardunias and Su, 2009b; Bardunias and Su, 2010; Fouquet et al., 2014; Green et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies: Bardunias and Su, 2009b; Bardunias and Su, 2010; Fouquet et al., 2014; Green et al., 2017.

claim: In Calovi et al., 2019, termites preferentially aggregate in concave regions of a surface and rearrange nest material at those locations.
source: For example, in Calovi et al., 2019 termites are shown to preferentially aggregate in concave regions of a surface and they would simply rearrange nest material (both digging and building) at those locations.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Calovi et al., 2019.

claim: Digging sites provide a template for pellet deposition.
source: Even if digging sites provide a template for pellet deposition (Fouquet et al., 2014; Green et al., 2017), and for this reason digging and construction often co-localize in space, it is clear that building and digging cannot completely overlap, or the two activities would simply cancel one the effect of the other: termites must be able to differentiate between the sites of these contrasting activities through digging- or building-specific cues.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fouquet et al., 2014 and Green et al., 2017.

claim: Termites must be able to differentiate between digging and building sites through specific cues.
source: Even if digging sites provide a template for pellet deposition (Fouquet et al., 2014; Green et al., 2017), and for this reason digging and construction often co-localize in space, it is clear that building and digging cannot completely overlap, or the two activities would simply cancel one the effect of the other: termites must be able to differentiate between the sites of these contrasting activities through digging- or building-specific cues.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the observation that digging and building cannot completely overlap.

claim: The model proposed in Ocko et al., 2019 indicates that a generic 'colony odor' undergoing advection and diffusion within the nest could provide a sufficient cue for determining the overall mound shape.
source: For example, the model proposed in Ocko et al., 2019 indicates that a generic 'colony odor' undergoing advection and diffusion within the nest could provide a sufficient cue for determining the overall mound shape, so leaving a possible role of a construction pheromone only for the structuring of small scale nest features such as pillars and walls.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ocko et al., 2019.

claim: Facchini et al., 2020 proposed a model in which small scale nest features can be produced in the absence of a construction pheromone by assuming that termites respond to the local curvature of emerging nest features.
source: Facchini et al., 2020 further proposed a model in which also small scale nest features can be produced in the absence of a construction pheromone, by assuming that termites respond to the local curvature of these emerging nest features.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Facchini et al., 2020.

claim: The building rules implemented in previous computational models are not empirically validated from direct observations of termite worker building behavior.
source: While these models reproduce a number of structures observed in real termite nests, the building rules implemented in the models are not empirically validated from direct observations of the building behavior of termite workers.
evidence: This is an inference about the state of validation for computational models.

claim: Pellet collection activity was distributed homogeneously all over the clay disk in the experiments.
source: Pellet collection activity was distributed homogeneously all over the clay disk that we provided at the center of the experimental arena.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Deposition activity was concentrated at the tips of pre-existing pillars and along the edges of the clay disk.
source: Conversely, deposition activity was concentrated at the tips of pre-existing pillars, and along the edges of the clay disk itself.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Termites do not show a preference for where they collect pellets.
source: Thus, termites do not show a preference for where they collect pellets while they target specific regions when depositing, which suggests that those regions must express a strong stimulus for deposition.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing homogeneous collection distribution.

claim: Termites target specific regions when depositing pellets.
source: Thus, termites do not show a preference for where they collect pellets while they target specific regions when depositing, which suggests that those regions must express a strong stimulus for deposition.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing concentrated deposition patterns.

claim: Occupancy is high close to the pillars and to the Petri dish walls in the experimental setup.
source: Occupancy is high close to the pillars and to the Petri dish walls, has intermediate values within the clay disk, and drops at the top of the pillars and right outside of the clay disk (i.e. precisely where deposits are recorded).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The top edge of the wall attracted many deposits, but pellet deposition focused at the wall tips in 7 out of 11 experiments.
source: We report that the top edge attracted many deposits, but pellet deposition focused at the wall tips pointing to curvature, rather than elevation, as the dominant cue in 7 out of 11 experiments (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data summarized in Table 1.

claim: Curvature, rather than elevation, is the dominant cue for pellet deposition.
source: We report that the top edge attracted many deposits, but pellet deposition focused at the wall tips pointing to curvature, rather than elevation, as the dominant cue in 7 out of 11 experiments (Table 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observation that depositions focused at wall tips (high curvature) rather than uniformly along the top edge (constant elevation).

claim: Experiments and simulations show a fair agreement as pellet depositions and initial growth concentrate in the same regions which are those where the surface is the most convex.
source: Experiments and simulations show a fair agreement as pellet depositions and initial growth concentrate in the same regions which are those where the surface is the most convex, as depicted in white in Figure 3C–F.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of experimental data with simulation results shown in Figures 2C and 3.

claim: The qualitative agreement between experimental results and curvature-based simulations supports the idea that surface curvature alone is a sufficient cue that could guide termite depositions.
source: The qualitative agreement between experimental results and curvature-based simulations supports the idea that, at least on a first approximation, surface curvature alone is a sufficient cue that could guide termite depositions.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison between experimental and simulation results.

claim: The clay disk is maintained constantly humid during experiments.
source: Trying to identify this additional building cue, we recall that the clay disk is maintained constantly humid.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup.

claim: The edges of the disk arena mark the limit between a humid region and the surrounding dry periphery.
source: The edges of the disk arena mark then the limit between a humid region and the surrounding dry periphery.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup.

claim: The clay tone remained unchanged during experiments which suggests that moisture is constantly evaporating from the clay disk while being replenished in water from below.
source: Also, the clay tone remained unchanged during experiments which suggests that moisture is constantly evaporating from the clay disk while being replenished in water from below, and that the overall process is stationary.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental observations.

claim: A net increase in humidity and a net decrease in temperature was observed coming from outside to inside the clay disk which is the footprint of evaporation.
source: We observed a net increase in humidity and a net decrease in temperature coming from outside to inside the clay disk which is the footprint of evaporation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Inside and outside the clay disk, both humidity and temperature remained relatively stable indicating that the system is roughly in a steady state.
source: Inside and outside the clay disk, both quantities remained relatively stable indicating that the system is roughly in a steady state.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Close enough to the evaporating substrate, humidity transport happens by diffusion.
source: Evaporation is a complex process, but close enough to the evaporating substrate, humidity transport happens by diffusion (Langmuir., 1918; Hisatake et al., 1993) and it is hence fully determined by the humidity gradient.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Langmuir., 1918 and Hisatake et al., 1993.

claim: Termites live in a viscous boundary layer where humidity transport is diffusive.
source: In agreement with previous studies (Soar et al., 2019), we can show with scaling arguments that our termites live in such a viscous boundary layer (see Appendix 3).
evidence: This is supported by scaling arguments in Appendix 3 and citation to Soar et al., 2019.

claim: In the diffusive regime, the evaporation flux is directly proportional to the surface curvature of the evaporating substrate.
source: In the diffusive regime, the evaporation flux is directly proportional to the surface curvature of the evaporating substrate (see Appendix 2 for a mathematical proof).
evidence: This is demonstrated through mathematical proof in Appendix 2.

claim: Curvature and evaporation are two completely interchangeable stimuli everywhere except at the edge of the clay disk.
source: As such, curvature and evaporation are two completely interchangeable stimuli everywhere except at the edge of the clay disk, where the transition between clay and perspex material corresponds to a strong humidity gradient in spite of weak surface curvature.
evidence: This is inferred from the computational analysis of humidity gradients and surface curvature.

claim: Evaporation flux can explain by itself the deposition patterns observed in the experiments.
source: We then propose that evaporation flux can explain by itself the deposition patterns observed in our experiments.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the correlation between evaporation patterns and deposition behavior.

claim: The distribution of salt deposits in chemical garden experiments matches very closely the regions of highest building activity by termites.
source: Remarkably the distribution of the salt deposits matches very closely the regions of highest building activity by termites, both being more pronounced at the edge of the clay disk and at the top of topographic cues (pillar and walls).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of chemical garden experiments (Figure 4C and D) with termite building patterns.

claim: Termite deposition probability covaries with the evaporation flux.
source: This result indicates that termite deposition probability covaries with the evaporation flux, which is consistent with our hypothesis of evaporation as the strongest cue for deposition.
evidence: This is inferred from the chemical garden experiments showing correlation between salt deposition (evaporation marker) and termite deposition patterns.

claim: Salt traces are less pronounced on the wall than on the pillars in chemical garden experiments.
source: One may notice that salt traces are less pronounced on the wall (Figure 4D) than on the pillars (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an observation from the chemical garden experiments shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The maximum amplitude of the humidity gradient is weaker in the wall case than in the pillar case.
source: This is consistent with the amplitude of the humidity gradient in a stationary diffusive regime as shown in Figure 4B and A respectively: the maximum amplitude of the gradient is weaker in the wall case.
evidence: This is supported by computational simulations shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The variability in termite construction patterns is larger in the case of wall cues compared to pillar cues.
source: Possibly, this could explain why in the case of wall cues there is a comparatively much larger variability in the patterns of termite construction (see Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from observations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: When termites are confronted with the 'wall' cue they are likely to start pellet depositions at the wall tips, but initial pellet depositions started at other locations on the top edge do also occur.
source: When termites are confronted with the 'wall' cue they are likely to start pellet depositions at the wall tips, but initial pellet depositions started at other locations on the top edge do also occur.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Initial pellet depositions are preserved and reinforced by positive feed-back mechanisms.
source: Whatever the initial choice, depositions are then preserved and reinforced by positive feed-back mechanisms which can lead to tightly selected deposition patterns also in the case of the 'wall' cue.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that initial deposition patterns persist and grow.

claim: The edge of the clay disk is almost flat for a termite walking across, but it is also a thin cusp of humid material which is strongly evaporating.
source: In fact, the edge of the clay disk is almost flat (weak convexity) for a termite walking across, but it is also a thin cusp (high convexity) of humid material which is strongly evaporating, similarly to what happens at the edge of a liquid drop and causes the formation of well known coffee stains (Deegan et al., 1997).
evidence: This is explained by analogy to coffee stain formation, supported by citation to Deegan et al., 1997.

claim: By providing loose and unmarked pellets, the study was able to prompt building activity without digging and to quantify collections and depositions as separate actions.
source: Here, by providing loose and unmarked pellets, we were able to prompt building activity without digging and to quantify collections and depositions as separate actions.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: All pellets were progressively displaced during the experiments.
source: We observed that all pellets were progressively displaced and that collections happened in a relatively random fashion.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Collections happened in a relatively random fashion.
source: We observed that all pellets were progressively displaced and that collections happened in a relatively random fashion.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing homogeneous collection distribution.

claim: Depositions concentrated at specific parts of the experimental arena which are the tips of the topographic cues and the edges of the clay disk.
source: On the contrary, depositions concentrated at specific parts of the experimental arena which are the tips of the topographic cues and the edges of the clay disk.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The conditional probability of deposition given termite occupancy was high at the tips of topographic cues and edges of the clay disk.
source: The conditional probability of deposition given termite occupancy was high there, indicating that those regions precisely drive termite depositions rather than generically attracting termite aggregation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The alternative use of pillars and walls as topographic cues allowed disentangling the role of elevation and curvature.
source: The alternative use of pillars and walls as topographic cues allowed us to disentangle the role of elevation and curvature and pointed toward curvature as the most attractive stimulus for deposition.
evidence: This describes the experimental design strategy.

claim: Surface curvature is a powerful morphogenetic organizer for 3D structure formation as it can drive the formation of pillars, walls and convoluted surfaces.
source: Surface curvature is a powerful morphogenetic organizer for 3D structure formation as it can drive the formation of pillars, walls and convoluted surfaces (Facchini et al., 2020), all features that are observed in the nests of various termite species.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Facchini et al., 2020 and general knowledge about termite nest structures.

claim: The study demonstrates a close coupling between surface curvature and the flux of evaporation from a surface.
source: Here, we were able to demonstrate a close coupling between surface curvature and the flux of evaporation from a surface, so providing a link to a possible stimulus sensed directly by termites.
evidence: This is supported by analytical derivations and experimental results shown in Figure 4.

claim: The findings reconcile previous discordant results pointing alternately to curvature or to humidity as the relevant stimuli.
source: This also allows us to reconcile previous discordant results pointing alternately to curvature (Calovi et al., 2019; Facchini et al., 2020) or to humidity (Soar et al., 2019; Bardunias et al., 2020) as the relevant stimuli.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the demonstrated relationship between curvature and evaporation, supported by citations.

claim: Langmuir., 1918 showed that close enough to the surface of a water droplet, evaporation scales as the inverse of the radius (i.e. as the mean curvature) of the droplet.
source: The idea itself of a relation between curvature and evaporation is not new, as already a century ago, Langmuir., 1918 showed that close enough to the surface of a water droplet, evaporation scales as the inverse of the radius (i.e. as the mean curvature) of the droplet see (Appendix 2 for a derivation).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Langmuir., 1918.

claim: Termites are particularly sensitive to the humidity of their environment because their small size and soft cuticle put them in constant danger of desiccation.
source: It is well known that termites are particularly sensitive to the humidity of their environment, because their small size and soft cuticle put them in constant danger of desiccation.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about termite physiology.

claim: Coptotermes termites can only survive in high-humidity environments such as moist wood or soil.
source: Coptotermes termites in particular are wetwood termites that can only survive in high-humidity environments such as moist wood or soil.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Coptotermes biology.

claim: In laboratory experiments, C. formosanus termites died within a few days when maintained at 72.9% or less relative humidity, but survived well when humidity was 98%.
source: For example, in laboratory experiments Zukowski and Su, 2017, C. formosanus termites died within a few days when maintained at 72.9% or less relative humidity, but survived well when humidity was 98%.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zukowski and Su, 2017.

claim: Coptotermes gestroi were able to discriminate between chambers with different relative humidity and, after 12 hr, almost all termites were in the highest humidity chamber (98%).
source: Coptotermes gestroi were also able to discriminate between chambers with different relative humidity and, after 12 hr, almost all termites were in the highest humidity chamber (98%), leaving the other chambers with 75% or less relative humidity empty (Gautam and Henderson, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gautam and Henderson, 2011.

claim: Given sufficient time, termites can detect a difference of humidity from 75% to 98% over a spatial scale of centimeters.
source: These results (which are similar also to other results testing termite response to chambers with different soil moisture) indicate that –given a sufficient amount of time– termites can detect a difference of humidity from 75% to 98% over a spatial scale of centimeters.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited experimental results.

claim: Humidity can affect termite behavior in the context of nest building by triggering nest expansion events.
source: Recent field and laboratory experiments have shown that humidity can affect termite behavior also in the context of nest building (Carey et al., 2019), by triggering nest expansion events (Bardunias et al., 2020; Carey et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Carey et al., 2019; Bardunias et al., 2020; Carey et al., 2021.

claim: Soar et al., 2019 showed that moisture flux affects termite building activity in terms of both pellet collection and deposition.
source: Even more interestingly, Soar et al., 2019 showed that moisture flux affects termite building activity (both in terms of pellet collection and deposition).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Soar et al., 2019.

claim: Moisture variations not only prompt or inhibit termite building activity, but constitute a local blueprint for construction.
source: Our experiments confirm this trend and suggest that moisture variations not only prompt or inhibit termite building activity, but constitute a local blueprint for construction.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results of the current study.

claim: The estimated humidity variations correspond to humidity variation of 10 to 100% across a distance not larger than termite body length.
source: As our termites are millimetre size, the estimated lower and upper boundary correspond to humidity variation of 10 to 100% across a distance not larger than their body length.
evidence: This is calculated from the estimated humidity gradients and termite body size.

claim: Humidity variations of 10 to 100% across termite body length must be sensed by termites.
source: We then expect that such variations must be sensed by termites, as they are larger than those that Coptotermes gestroi termites were shown to be able to discriminate over much larger spatial scales in the experiments reviewed above.
evidence: This is inferred by comparing calculated humidity gradients with previously reported termite sensory capabilities.

claim: The experiments do not support a role for a putative cement pheromone added by termites to the building material.
source: Our experiments do not support a role for a putative cement pheromone, added by termites to the building material, which would stimulate pellet depositions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results showing construction on unmarked materials.

claim: Construction occurred reliably on provided building cues even if they only comprised fresh clay and sterilized pellets with no pheromone markings.
source: In fact, construction occurred reliably on our provided building cues, even if they only comprised fresh clay and sterilized pellets with no pheromone markings.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Simulations indicate that qualitatively similar construction results can be obtained without assuming a role for construction pheromone.
source: Our simulations further indicate that qualitatively similar construction results can be obtained without assuming a role for construction pheromone.
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3.

claim: The influence of a cement pheromone can be excluded, at least during the early choice of the deposition sites.
source: We can hence exclude the influence of a cement pheromone, at least during the early choice of the deposition sites, in agreement with recent experiments by other authors (Fouquet et al., 2014; Petersen et al., 2015; Green et al., 2017).
evidence: This conclusion is supported by the current experimental results and citations to other studies.

claim: In the experiments, the building substrate was constantly moist throughout the entire duration of the experiments.
source: We should point to the fact, however, that in our experiments the building substrate was constantly moist throughout the entire duration of the experiments.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental conditions.

claim: Under conditions where moisture may not constantly replenish the porous wall, the evaporation flux is maintained by the humidity that is naturally embedded in recently dropped pellets.
source: We suggest that under these conditions, the evaporation flux is maintained by the humidity that is naturally embedded in recently dropped pellets, which makes the construction process self-sustainable and is consistent with the hypothesis of a viscous boundary layer extending with termite activity (Soar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about construction in natural conditions, supported by citation to Soar et al., 2019.

claim: It would be very hard to distinguish between a scenario where evaporation is maintained by pellet humidity and one which involves a putative cement pheromone added directly to manipulated pellets by termites.
source: In practice, it would be very hard to distinguish between such a scenario and one which involves a putative cement pheromone added directly to manipulated pellets by termites.
evidence: This is a speculation about the difficulty of distinguishing between alternative mechanisms.

claim: Pheromones may play a role in termite building behavior by mediating termite aggregation.
source: More generally, while we do not rule out a possible role of pheromones in termite building behavior (mediating for instance termite aggregation), we have shown that pheromones are not necessary to explain the early deposition patterns that we see in our experiments.
evidence: This is a speculation about possible roles of pheromones not tested in the current study.

claim: Pheromones are not necessary to explain the early deposition patterns observed in the experiments.
source: More generally, while we do not rule out a possible role of pheromones in termite building behavior (mediating for instance termite aggregation), we have shown that pheromones are not necessary to explain the early deposition patterns that we see in our experiments.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results and simulations.

claim: Collective nest construction is a dynamic process and the deposition of new pellets by termites constantly changes the shape and the porosity of the evaporating substrate.
source: In this study, we have focused on understanding how termites respond to well-controlled predefined stimuli. However, collective nest construction is a dynamic process and the deposition of new pellets by termites constantly changes the shape and the porosity of the evaporating substrate, potentially affecting nest growth through positive or negative feedback.
evidence: This is a general statement about the dynamic nature of nest construction.

claim: Termites can control the size of the pellets used for nest construction, and indirectly also the porosity of nest walls.
source: Recent studies have shown that termites can control the size of the pellets used for nest construction, and indirectly also the porosity of nest walls (Zachariah et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zachariah et al., 2017.

claim: Substrate porosity plays an important role for ventilation and drainage of the nest.
source: In turn, substrate porosity is known to play an important role for ventilation and drainage of the nest (Singh et al., 2019) and the moisture content of pellets can also affect the mechanical properties of the mound itself (Zachariah et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Singh et al., 2019.

claim: The moisture content of pellets can affect the mechanical properties of the mound.
source: In turn, substrate porosity is known to play an important role for ventilation and drainage of the nest (Singh et al., 2019) and the moisture content of pellets can also affect the mechanical properties of the mound itself (Zachariah et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zachariah et al., 2020.

claim: The conclusions are relatively robust to changes in substrate porosity and moisture content.
source: In relation to our own experiments, however, our scaling analyses (Appendix 3) indicate that our conclusions are relatively robust to changes in substrate porosity and moisture content.
evidence: This is based on scaling analyses presented in Appendix 3.

claim: Porosity only controls the time scale of water uptake from the reservoir by capillary rise.
source: For example, porosity only controls the time scale of water uptake from the reservoir by capillary rise, which must be small enough to keep the clay disk hydrated, and this assumption remains valid up to mm-size pores in the new construction.
evidence: This is based on scaling analysis in Appendix 3.

claim: The addition of new pellets to regions of high convexity is likely to make the surface less smooth than the initial topography.
source: Similarly, for local curvature, the addition of new pellets to regions of high convexity is likely to make the surface less smooth than the initial topography, and such additional 'roughness' can only increase the effect of focusing evaporation at those locations.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the effect of pellet addition on surface roughness.

claim: Additional roughness from pellet addition can only increase the effect of focusing evaporation at locations of high convexity.
source: Similarly, for local curvature, the addition of new pellets to regions of high convexity is likely to make the surface less smooth than the initial topography, and such additional 'roughness' can only increase the effect of focusing evaporation at those locations.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the effect of roughness on evaporation.

claim: Calovi et al., 2019 pointed to an effect of surface curvature on termite construction behavior.
source: Previous work by Calovi et al., 2019 had pointed to an effect of surface curvature on termite construction behavior.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Calovi et al., 2019.

claim: In Calovi et al., 2019, pellet depositions are attracted by convex features, while termite activity was concentrated at regions of maximum concavity.
source: While our two studies emphasize the same point, we should note that our results and the results reported in Calovi et al., 2019 are not entirely consistent, because in our experiments, pellet depositions are attracted by convex features, while in Calovi et al., 2019 termite activity was concentrated at regions of maximum concavity.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current study results and those reported in Calovi et al., 2019.

claim: The measure in Calovi et al., 2019 is a correlation between concavity and digging activity, not building.
source: As this previous study did not distinguish digging from deposition activity, we believe that their measure is a correlation between concavity and digging activity, not building.
evidence: This is an inference about the interpretation of results from Calovi et al., 2019.

claim: Concave regions should attract digging activity as predicted by the model.
source: The fact that concave regions should attract digging activity is predicted by our model (see Materials and methods) and was visible also in our experiments where concavity (Figure 3D) attracted digging at the base of wall-like cues (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by model predictions and experimental observations shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Termites dig along the humidity gradient, that is toward the most humid region.
source: Note that such behavior can be interpreted as termites digging along the humidity gradient, that is toward the most humid region.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed digging behavior.

claim: In the absence of loose pellets, spontaneous digging usually started right above the hydration holes of the setup.
source: Accordingly, in many preliminary experiments we observed that, in the absence of loose pellets, spontaneous digging usually started right above the hydration holes of our setup (Figure 3B) as a further confirmation of the termite ability to sense and respond to humidity gradients.
evidence: This is supported by observations from preliminary experiments.

claim: Termites would focus pellet depositions at regions of strong evaporation flux as a general mechanism capable of organizing termite building activity.
source: In our study, we have outlined a general mechanism capable of organizing termite building activity: termites would focus pellet depositions at regions of strong evaporation flux.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on experimental and analytical results.

claim: The building rule is embedded in the shape itself of the nest internal structure.
source: In turn, evaporation flux co-varies with surface curvature, which implies that the building rule is embedded in the shape itself of the nest internal structure.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the demonstrated relationship between curvature and evaporation.

claim: The nests built by termites of different genera or species show a large diversity of forms.
source: The nests built by termites of different genera or species show a large diversity of forms (see e.g. Grassé, 1984), which indicates that the nest-building process should also be different.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grassé, 1984 and general knowledge.

claim: The nest-building process should be different for different termite species.
source: The nests built by termites of different genera or species show a large diversity of forms (see e.g. Grassé, 1984), which indicates that the nest-building process should also be different.
evidence: This is inferred from the diversity of nest forms.

claim: The nest building behavior of termites must rely on more complex 'building rules' than the simple ones highlighted in this study.
source: Arguably, the nest building behavior of termites, shaped by millions of years of evolution, must rely on more complex 'building rules' than the simple ones highlighted here.
evidence: This is a speculation about the complexity of natural nest building.

claim: The nests built by all termite species rely on a small number of architectural elements such as pillars and branching surfaces.
source: Nonetheless, it is interesting to notice that the nests built by all species rely on a small number of architectural elements such as pillars and branching surfaces.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge about termite nest architecture.

claim: Simple variation of the basic building pattern coupled with variation of substrate evaporation would be sufficient to explain a large part of termite nest diversity.
source: We can imagine that, perhaps, simple variation of the basic building pattern described here, coupled with variation of the substrate evaporation itself (e.g. under the effect of air currents, the properties of the building material, and heat produced by the colony itself) would still be sufficient to explain a large part of termite nest diversity.
evidence: This is a speculation about the generalizability of the findings.

claim: Ocko et al., 2019 showed that a single mechanism can be responsible for determining the overall shape of nests made by various species.
source: Ocko et al., 2019 have already shown that a single mechanism can be responsible for determining the overall shape of nests made by various species: perhaps an equally simple general mechanism can account for the even larger variation of internal nest structure.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ocko et al., 2019.

claim: Many biological structures at the microscopic scale present convoluted structures that appear via tip growth and branching phenomena.
source: Beyond the field of termite architecture, many other biological structures, particularly at the microscopic scale, present convoluted structures that appear via tip growth and branching phenomena.
evidence: This is general knowledge about biological morphogenesis.

claim: The morphogenesis of biological structures may rely on the coupling between the local curvature of the growing substrate and the localization of cues that stimulate the growth.
source: Similar to termite nests, the morphogenesis of these structures may rely on the coupling between the local curvature of the growing substrate and the localization of cues that stimulate the growth.
evidence: This is a speculation about general principles of biological morphogenesis based on the termite findings.

claim: There is a growing consensus that local curvature can affect cell migrations, cell patterning and tissue growth typically by direct mechanical sensing through the cytoskeleton.
source: Generally, there is a growing consensus today on the fact that local curvature can affect cell migrations, cell patterning and tissue growth typically by direct mechanical sensing through the cytoskeleton (Pieuchot et al., 2018; Callens et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pieuchot et al., 2018 and Callens et al., 2023.

claim: Curvature guidance can act indirectly by focusing the gradient of a diffusing quantity that promotes substrate growth.
source: However, analogous mechanisms to those described here can also explain tip growth and branching in mammal lungs, Clément et al., 2012, and reconnections in the gastrovascular networks of jellyfishes Song et al., 2023, the common feature being that curvature guidance acts indirectly, by focusing the gradient of a diffusing quantity that promotes the substrate growth.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Clément et al., 2012 and Song et al., 2023.

claim: Coptotermes gestroi is a soil-nesting wood-feeding termite originating from South-East Asia.
source: Coptotermes gestroi is a soil-nesting wood-feeding termite originating from South-East Asia (Li et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2010.

claim: Coptotermes gestroi has spread to Asia and other parts of the world including Africa, Europe, North America, Central America and South America as a result of increased global human activity.
source: However, as a result of the increase of global human activity, it has spread in Asia and to other parts of the world including Africa, Europe, North America, Central America and South America (Su et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Su et al., 2017.

claim: As an exotic pest, Coptotermes gestroi is primarily found in populated urban environments where it feeds on human-made structures.
source: As an exotic pest it is primarily found in populated urban environments, where it feeds on human-made structures (Su et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Su et al., 2003.

claim: In its natural habitat, C. gestroi feed on dead trees and wooden debris on the soil surface and build their nest underground.
source: In its natural habitat C. gestroi feed on dead trees and wooden debris on the soil surface and build their nest underground, although 'aerial' infestations have also been recorded in human made structures, where the nest have no contact with the ground.
evidence: This is general knowledge about C. gestroi biology.

claim: The internal nest structure of C. gestroi comprises a 'scaffold' of interconnected pillars.
source: Whether the nest is aerial or subterranean, the internal nest structure is similar to the nests of other termites in the Coptotermes genus, and comprises a 'scaffold' of interconnected pillars (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by observation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The scaffold structure of C. gestroi nests is the result of a building process.
source: This structure is the result of a building process, as evidenced by the fact that its material composition is different from the composition of the surrounding soil and comprises some stercoral carton.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference in material composition.

claim: Colonies of C. gestroi are estimated to be within the range of 100,000–4,000,000 individuals.
source: Colonies of C. gestroi are estimated to be within the range of 100,000–4,000,000 individuals (Ab Majid and Ahmad, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ab Majid and Ahmad, 2015.

evidence: This describes the source of experimental subjects.

source: For most experiments, termites were collected from the same master captive colony (c22) of Coptotermes gestroi hosted at the LEEC laboratory (Villetaneuse, France) in a tropical room with constant temperature (26 ± 2°C) and relative humidity (70 ± 10%).
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions.
